author: Diptanu Choudhury
text: We are seeing backlash against sandboxes for primarily a couple of reasons - vendors don't support users to overcommit compute. You can't pay for N cores and overcommit the number of sandboxes that are run on those cores. In reality agents don't uniformly use resources during their lifecycle...
suggestedEngagement: Agree and extend: 'We see the same with orchestration workloads — peak at task dispatch, idle 80% of runtime. Pay-per-core models penalize exactly this pattern. Is there a vendor you've seen get the pricing model right?'
Ask a sharp follow-up: 'Do you think overcommit will come from sandbox vendors themselves, or from a scheduling layer above them? Curious whether Tensorlake is building in that direction.'
Challenge gently: 'Feels like a pricing model problem more than a sandbox problem — is the right fix time-sliced billing or true overcommit with QoS guarantees?'

author: Thomas Roccia
text: Coding Agents. The Insider Threat You Installed Yourself — argues that coding agents with terminal access and the ability to trigger real system actions represent an underappreciated insider-threat surface. Also recently published NOVA Tracer: a security monitoring layer for Claude Code that detects prompt injection and generates full HTML audit reports.
suggestedEngagement: Validate with a specific scenario: 'The supply-chain angle is the scary part — a poisoned MCP server or malicious file in the repo can instruct the agent silently. Have you seen injections coming through dependencies rather than direct user input?'
Reference the NOVA Tracer work: 'Your audit trail approach is exactly the right instinct — observability before trust. Are you planning to open the detection ruleset, or is it tied to OpenClaw?'
Ask about enterprise adoption: 'How are enterprise security teams responding — writing agent usage policies, or still mostly unaware of the agent-level attack surface?'

author: Carlos E. Perez
text: Researchers gave AI agents real email accounts, Discord access, and shell commands for 2 weeks. They deleted mail servers 'for security.' They leaked secrets. They gaslit each other. Here are 11 vulnerabilities that should terrify anyone deploying autonomous AI — covers owner spoofing, resource exhaustion, inter-agent vulnerability propagation, and provider value bleed-through.
suggestedEngagement: Highlight enterprise implication: 'The inter-agent propagation finding is the most alarming for enterprise deployments — one compromised agent poisoning a whole mesh. Is there a clean architectural pattern in the research for containing blast radius?'

Connect to identity/authorization gap: 'Owner spoofing is essentially an authentication gap — agents need cryptographically verified identity chains, not just natural language claims. Did the research test capability-based or token-bound identity schemes?'
Ask about model variation: 'Were the vulnerabilities consistent across Claude Opus and Kimi K2.5, or did one show meaningfully better resistance to owner spoofing and constitutional poisoning?'
